endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Across these approaches, relevant considerations might include whether the device performs consistently across clinically relevant subgroups within the intended use population.

evidence.title: Clinical assessment of an AI tool for measuring biventricular parameters on cardiac MR
evidence.outcome: Radiologist visual review of AI-generated contours for accuracy
evidence.effect: Contours evaluated visually in 251 cases; agreement or minor disagreement in 229 (91.2%); failed segmentation in a single case (0.4%).
evidence.quote: The automated contours were evaluated visually in 251 cases, with agreement or minor disagreement in 229 cases (91.2%) and failed segmentation in only a single case (0.4%).

evidence.title: Prospective blinded clinical evaluation of a fully automated workflow for prostate radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Blinded board-certified oncologist ratings of real patient AI-generated plans and structure sets as good/acceptable/unacceptable
evidence.effect: Clinically acceptable results in 86% of fully automated cases vs 95% conventional; automated plans rated 'good' less often (12/22 vs 17/22), mainly due to smaller target delineation.
evidence.quote: Clinically acceptable results were achieved in 86% of fully automated cases compared with 95% in the conventional workflow.

evidence.title: Prospective evaluation of a large language model clinical decision support system in the emergency department
evidence.outcome: Expert clinician review of sampled real AI outputs for clinical appropriateness
evidence.effect: Expert review rated 99 of 100 sampled outputs as clinically appropriate; no adverse events detected.
evidence.quote: No adverse events were detected, and expert review rated 99 of 100 sampled outputs as clinically appropriate.

evidence.title: Leveraging artificial intelligence to summarize abstracts in lay language for increasing research accessibility and transparency
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Researcher review of AI lay summary sentences for accuracy, relevance, and harmfulness
evidence.effect: 95.9% accuracy (95% CI 92.1-97.9) and 96.2% relevance (92.4-98.1) across 192 sentences from 33 abstracts; none deemed harmful.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT achieved 95.9% (95% CI, 92.1-97.9) accuracy and 96.2% (92.4-98.1) relevance across 192 summary sentences from 33 abstracts based on researcher review.
evidence.sample_unit: abstracts (192 summary sentences reviewed by researchers; 34 volunteers rated accessibility/transparency)

evidence.title: Evolution of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Application for Mammography
evidence.outcome: Functional testing findings
evidence.effect: Initial expert radiologist review of AI outputs identified missing labels and inappropriate use of color graphic masks.
evidence.quote: Initial functional testing of the AI model (version 0.14.0) revealed two inconsistencies with the Baseline Functional Requirements: (1) absence of a “For research purposes only” label in both DICOM SR and additional image series, and (2) using color graphic masks to highlight pathological findings ( Figure 4 ).

evidence.title: Use of a Generative Pretrained Transformer to Answer Questions and Facilitate a Large Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Heart Association
evidence.outcome: Manual review of real GPT answers to site questions for helpfulness, completeness, and accuracy
evidence.effect: Of 588 GPT-answered questions, 13 (2%) not helpful, 12 (2%) incomplete, 5 (1%) misleading, 3 (1%) correct but with conflicting messaging.
evidence.quote: On manual review, of the 588 that the GPT reportedly answered, only 13 (2%) were not helpful responses, 12 (2%) were incomplete responses, 5 (1%) were misleading, and 3 (1%) contained the correct response but also provided some conflicting messaging.

evidence.title: Personalizing prostate cancer education for patients using an EHR-Integrated LLM agent
evidence.outcome: Clinician review of real patient-chat histories for correctness, completeness, safety, and personalization
evidence.effect: Clinicians rated MedEduChat as highly correct (2.9/3), complete (2.7/3), and safe (2.7/3), with moderate personalization (2.3/3).
evidence.quote: Clinicians evaluated the patient-chat interaction history and rated MedEduChat as highly correct (2.9/3), complete (2.7/3), and safe (2.7/3), with moderate personalization (2.3/3).

evidence.title: Improving support and self-management of ophthalmic patients using an artificial intelligence health coach
evidence.outcome: Independent glaucoma consultant validation of AI question-answer pairs across assessed domains
evidence.effect: Human expert validation scores exceeded 95% across all assessed domains.
evidence.quote: Human expert validation scores exceeded 95% across all assessed domains.
evidence.sample_unit: patients who interacted with the AI health coach (446 chat sessions analyzed)

evidence.title: Assessing the quality of AI-generated and physician-written discharge summaries: evaluation of an EHR-integrated tool in a Dutch academic hospital
evidence.outcome: Blinded clinician ratings of LLM discharge summaries vs physician-written on completeness, correctness, conciseness, trust
evidence.effect: LLM summaries had lower completeness (4.50 vs 5.00; p<0.001), similar correctness (p=0.14); trusted in 85.3%, partially trusted 11.6%, rejected 3.1% of cases.
evidence.quote: Physician-written summaries were trusted by both reviewers in 279 (95.5%) cases, whereas LLM-generated summaries were trusted in 249 (85.3%) cases, partially trusted in 34 (11.6%), and rejected in 9 (3.1%).

evidence.title: Development and Clinical Evaluation of a Large Language Model-Based System for Generating Patient-Friendly Echocardiography Reports: Two-Stage Retrospective Validation and Prospective Survey Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician and external LLM quality ratings of generated reports on real patient data
evidence.effect: Total scores 18.15 (SD 1.36) clinicians vs 18.28 (SD 1.26) external LLM, P=.55; one hallucination event identified in 60 reports.
evidence.quote: Professional evaluation showed high overall quality scores from both clinicians and the external LLM, with no significant difference between evaluators (mean total scores 18.15, SD 1.36 vs 18.28, SD 1.26; P=.55).
evidence.sample_unit: patients (prospective stage; 60 patients in retrospective stage)

evidence.title: Automated Post-Analytical Workflow for Newborn Screening Using a Hybrid Rule-Based and Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model System
evidence.outcome: Specialist review of AI-generated report drafts for clinically meaningful errors
evidence.effect: Across 20 synthetic cases representing 10 disorders, five specialists identified no major errors affecting clinical interpretation.
evidence.quote: Across 20 synthetic cases representing 10 disorders, five specialists identified no major errors affecting clinical interpretation.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic cases (report drafts reviewed by 5 specialists)

evidence.title: Clinical Implementation and Validation of Automated Slice-to-Volume Reconstruction for Fetal MRI Using a Vendor-Neutral MONAI-Based Imaging Informatics Pipeline
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.outcome: Radiologist-rated quality of reconstructed outputs on real examinations
evidence.effect: Three fellowship-trained fetal radiologists independently scored reconstructions; brain SVR pass-or-higher in 59/65 (90.8%), body 57/65 (87.7%); ICC 0.93 brain, 0.92 body.
evidence.quote: Brain SVR was rated pass-or-higher in 59/65 examinations (90.8%) and body SVR was rated pass-or-higher in 57/65 examinations (87.7%).

evidence.title: Clinical Validation of Medical-based Large Language Model Chatbots on Ophthalmic Patient Queries with LLM-based Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Agreement between GPT-4-Turbo grading and ophthalmologist grading of LLM responses
evidence.effect: GPT-4-Turbo grading aligned strongly with clinicians (Spearman rho 0.80, Kendall tau 0.67); Senior Consultants graded more conservatively, supporting hybrid automated and clinician review.
evidence.quote: GPT-4-Turbo grading showed strong alignment with clinician assessments overall, with Spearman rho of 0.80 and Kendall tau of 0.67, though Senior Consultants graded more conservatively.
evidence.sample_unit: model responses to ophthalmology patient queries

evidence.title: MetaPlate: Counterfactual-Guided RAG-LLM Tool for Personalized Food Recommendation and Hyperglycemia Prevention
evidence.outcome: Registered dietitian review of LLM meal recommendations for realism and suitability, before vs after prompt refinement
evidence.effect: Improvements in meal realism, portion suitability, and recommendation likelihood; expert feedback showed a shift from clinically implausible outputs to actionable, contextually appropriate recommendations.
evidence.quote: Results show improvements in meal realism, portion suitability, and recommendation likelihood, with expert feedback indicating a shift from clinically implausible outputs to actionable, contextually appropriate recommendations.
evidence.sample_unit: meal recommendations rated by registered dietitians

evidence.title: Evaluating AI Generated Summaries for Cancer Patients
evidence.outcome: Whether expert clinician review of AI cancer summaries identifies inaccuracies and omissions
evidence.effect: Expert review identified limitations in generated summaries, such as occasional omissions and minor inaccuracies, which were used to improve prompts, grounding, and guardrails.
evidence.quote: Some limitations were identified in the generated summaries e.g., occasional omissions and minor inaccuracies.

evidence.title: Internal Validation of a Machine Learning Model for Antimicrobial Stewardship: Evaluating Trainability of Data and the Accuracy of Clinical Recommendations Within a Clinical Decision Support System
evidence.outcome: Independent clinician review of ML recommendations against standard guidelines for discrepancies
evidence.effect: Among 644 clinician-trained reports, no major discrepancies in recommendations, with only 100 showing minor differences.
evidence.quote: Among 644 clinician-trained reports, there were no major discrepancies in recommendations, with only 100 showing minor differences.

evidence.title: Evaluating the acceptability, usability and clinical appropriateness of  Your Path  , an AI-powered tool facilitating relevant access to HIV services post-HIV self-testing in South Africa
evidence.outcome: Clinician appraisal of appropriateness of AI conversation summaries from real user interaction transcripts
evidence.effect: HCPs reviewed transcripts of CM tool interactions and found the conversational summaries clinically appropriate, informative and beneficial for supporting linkage to HIV care.
evidence.quote: HCPs found the conversational summaries clinically appropriate, and cited the tool as informative and beneficial for supporting linkage to HIV care.

evidence.title: Large Language Model Performance in UK Advice & Guidance: A Pilot Study in Neurology
evidence.outcome: Whether clinician review of real queries and LLM responses detects unsafe outputs (tail risk)
evidence.effect: No significant aggregate differences between blinded neurologist and LLM responses, but 10% of LLM responses received concerning scores (≤2 average) vs 0% of human responses.
evidence.quote: However, aggregate metrics masked clinically important edge-case failures in LLM responses.

evidence.title: Clinician-Centered Evaluation of Large Language Model-Generated Discharge Summaries for Longer Hospitalizations: Insights from Hospitalists and Primary Care Physicians
evidence.outcome: Clinician review of real patient records and LLM outputs for accuracy and safety
evidence.effect: Clinician reviewers preferred LLM summaries for 95% of encounters and rated them higher for quality, readability, factuality and completeness; PCPs identified more omissions with greater harm likelihood than hospitalists.
evidence.quote: Clinician reviewers preferred LLM-generated summaries for 95% of encounters and rated them higher for quality, readability, factuality and completeness.

evidence.title: Quantifying Cancer Clinical Trial Eligibility Using Artificial Intelligence-Based Matching
evidence.outcome: Effect of physician edits to LLM-generated SQL eligibility code on eligibility determinations
evidence.effect: Physician edits to generated SQL did not change any of 720 trial-patient eligibility determinations for 24 synthetic patients across 30 trials.
evidence.quote: In physician review of 30 trials, edits to generated SQL did not change any of 720 trial-patient eligibility determinations for 24 synthetic patients.

evidence.title: Evaluating Methods for Assessing LLM-Translated Clinical Discharge Instructions: A Comparison of Automated Metrics, MQM-Based Evaluation, and Clinician Review
evidence.outcome: Need for clinician translation review
evidence.effect: Variable translation quality; accuracy and terminology remained important areas for clinician assessment.
evidence.quote: LLM-generated Spanish discharge instructions demonstrated variable translation quality depending on the evaluation approach, with accuracy and terminology remaining important areas for clinician assessment.

evidence.title: LUMANA: A Scenario-Based Field Validation of a Culturally Adapted AI System for Mental Health Screening in Sokoto State, Nigeria
evidence.outcome: Clinician ratings of AI output safety across standardized scenarios
evidence.effect: 113/136 (83%) AI outputs acceptable as shown; 23/136 (17%) acceptable only with human review; none unacceptable.
evidence.quote: Overall, 113/136 (83%) AI outputs were rated acceptable as shown, while 23/136 (17%) were considered acceptable only with human review; no AI output was rated unacceptable.
evidence.sample_unit: stakeholders completing structured evaluations (136 AI output safety assessments across 8 scenarios)

evidence.title: Clinical implementation and evaluation of deep learning-assisted automatic radiotherapy treatment planning for lung cancer
evidence.outcome: Expert clinician review of AI-generated plans for clinical acceptability
evidence.effect: Automatic plans clinically acceptable in 88% of reviews (176/200) by four expert reviewers; all accepted after fine tuning.
evidence.quote: In qualitative evaluation, automatic plans were deemed to be clinically acceptable for treatment in 88% of reviews (176/200), and all were accepted after fine tuning.

evidence.title: Real-World Evaluation of Large Language Models in Healthcare (RWE-LLM): A New Realm of AI Safety & Validation
evidence.outcome: Tiered clinician review of AI call outputs and resulting safety improvement
evidence.effect: 6,234 licensed clinicians reviewed >307,000 calls; incorrect advice with potential minor harm decreased from 1.32% to 0.13% and 0.07%, severe harm concerns eliminated.
evidence.quote: Incorrect advice resulting in potential minor harm decreased from 1.32% to 0.13% and 0.07%, and severe harm concerns were eliminated (0.06% to 0.10% and 0.00%).

evidence.title: Clinical evaluation of a deep learning segmentation model including manual adjustments afterwards for locally advanced breast cancer
evidence.venue: Technical innovations & patient support in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Clinician qualitative scoring of AI contours as clinically acceptable, with or without corrections
evidence.effect: 92% of auto-contours were scored clinically acceptable with or without correction; CTVp unusable in seven cases, CTVn1 in six, CTVn4 in four.
evidence.quote: During qualitative measurements, the auto-contours got scored as clinical acceptable, with or without corrections, in 92% of the cases.

evidence.title: Comparison of Ophthalmologist and Large Language Model Chatbot Responses to Online Patient Eye Care Questions
evidence.outcome: Masked ophthalmologist panel rating of chatbot vs human answers for incorrect information and harm
evidence.effect: Chatbot answers comparable to human answers for incorrect/inappropriate material (PR 0.92; 95% CI 0.77-1.10), likelihood of harm (PR 0.84; 0.67-1.07), extent of harm (PR 0.99; 0.80-1.22).
evidence.quote: The likelihood of chatbot answers containing incorrect or inappropriate material was comparable with human answers (PR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.77-1.10), and did not differ from human answers in terms of likelihood of harm (PR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.67-1.07) nor extent of harm (PR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.80-1.22).
evidence.sample_unit: patient questions with paired chatbot and ophthalmologist answers

evidence.title: Real-world validation of Artificial Intelligence-based Computed Tomography auto-contouring for prostate cancer radiotherapy planning
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: clinician review of automatic contours
evidence.effect: Review found segmentation not fully satisfactory in 2/20 and 3/20 patients, requiring more extensive editing.
evidence.quote: Despite the excellent performances, in a limited fraction of patients the segmentation was not fully satisfactory (2 and 3 out of 20 patients for the two observers, respectively), requiring more extensive editing for a few patients.

evidence.title: Framework for Radiation Oncology Department-wide Evaluation and Implementation of Commercial Artificial Intelligence Autocontouring
evidence.outcome: Blinded expert clinician Likert ratings of AI-generated contours
evidence.effect: Multiple experts rated blinded AI contours; 70.7% (AI1) and 74.6% (AI2) of ROIs acceptable with at most minor edits across 2906 ratings; H&N lower (29.0/35.6%).
evidence.quote: Qualitative assessment was performed by multiple experts scoring blinded AI-contours using a Likert scale.
evidence.sample_unit: patient planning CT scans (859 clinically approved contours)

evidence.title: Automatic gross tumor volume segmentation with failure detection for safe implementation in locally advanced cervical cancer
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Clinician review of AI segmentations of real patient images against predefined A/B/C criteria
evidence.effect: Oncologist scored 62% (32/51) A, 27% (14/51) B, 5% (3/51) C; 2 declined for low quality; mean correction time 4.26 min vs about 16 min manual.
evidence.quote: Additionally, based on qualitative results, specifically, 62% (32/51), 27% (14/51), and 5% (3/51) of the images in the test set (cohort 2) were scored as A, B, and C, respectively.

evidence.title: Viability of Open Large Language Models for Clinical Documentation in German Health Care: Real-World Model Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Independent human rater usability of generated reports on real-world data
evidence.effect: 95 (93.1%) of 102 reports generated by the selected model were rated usable as is or with only minor changes by both human raters.
evidence.quote: In the manual evaluation by human experts, 95 (93.1%) of the 102 reports generated by that model were evaluated as usable as is or with only minor changes by both human raters.

evidence.title: The Treasure Trove Hidden in Plain Sight: The Utility of GPT-4 in Chest Radiograph Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Expert review of GPT-4 ADA outputs detecting statistical errors and inaccuracies
evidence.effect: Expert validation (methodology check, code quality, re-execution) found largely appropriate outputs but identified some statistical errors and inaccuracies.
evidence.quote: While GPT-4 ADA provided largely appropriate visualizations, descriptive statistical measures, quantitative statistical associations based on logistic regression, and gradient boosting machines for the predictive task (AUC, 0.75), some statistical errors and inaccuracies were encountered.

evidence.title: Evaluating the pathological and clinical implications of errors made by an artificial intelligence colon biopsy screening tool
evidence.outcome: Clinical impact of AI false-negative errors on patients, as scored by expert pathological and clinical review
evidence.effect: 220 FN errors across 164 cases (4.4% of WSI, 7.9% of cases); 88.4% of FN errors would have no impact on patient care, with only one error causing major patient harm.
evidence.quote: 88.4% of FN errors would have no impact on patient care, with only one error causing major patient harm.

evidence.title: A dataset and benchmark for hospital course summarization with adapted large language models
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Clinician reader preference versus automated summarization metrics for LLM-generated hospital course summaries
evidence.effect: Despite comparable quantitative metrics, clinicians significantly preferred GPT-4 in-context summaries over fine-tuned Llama2-13B and original summaries (P<.001), showing metrics alone missed quality differences.
evidence.quote: Despite comparable quantitative metrics, the reader study depicts a significant preference for summaries generated by GPT-4 with in-context learning compared to both Llama2-13B fine-tuned summaries and the original summaries (P<.001), highlighting the need for qualitative clinical evaluation.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical note/BHC samples rated by 5 clinicians

evidence.title: Abdominal and Pelvic MRI Protocol Prediction Using Natural Language Processing
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.outcome: Expert review of model protocol errors to judge whether they were correct or reasonable alternatives
evidence.effect: Expert review found 81.9% of errors were correct or reasonable alternative protocols, raising real-world accuracy from 88.5% to 97.9%.
evidence.quote: Subsequent expert review of the errors performed to satisfy departmental leadership showed 81.9% were in fact correct or reasonable alternative protocols, yielding real-world performance accuracy of 97.9%.

evidence.title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Generate Clinical Histories for Oncologic Imaging Requisitions
evidence.outcome: Radiologist review of LLM-generated histories against reference standard and original histories for quality and harm
evidence.effect: GPT-4 extracted oncologic parameters from clinical notes with F1 = 0.983; 10 radiologists preferred LLM histories 89% vs 5% and rated lower likelihood of harm (3% vs 55%).
evidence.quote: Radiologists preferred LLM-generated histories for imaging interpretation (89% vs 5%, 7% equal; P < .001), indicating they would enable more complete interpretation (86% vs 0%, 15% equal; P < .001) and have a lower likelihood of harm (3% vs 55%, 42% neither; P < .001).

evidence.title: Validation of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Virtual Assistant for Emergency Triage in Neurology
evidence.outcome: Neurologist agreement with AI outputs on real patient inputs and assistant recommendations
evidence.effect: Neurologists agreed with VA in 98.5% of cases for syndromic diagnosis; definitive diagnosis always in top 5 differentials; agreed with all diagnostic parameters and recommendations in stage 2.
evidence.quote: In stage 1, neurologists agreed with the VA in 98.5% of the cases for syndromic diagnosis, and in all cases, the definitive diagnosis was among the top 5 differentials.

evidence.title: Retrospective Comparative Analysis of Prostate Cancer In-Basket Messages: Responses From Closed-Domain Large Language Models Versus Clinical Teams
evidence.outcome: Clinician-graded completeness, correctness, clarity, empathy of LLM drafts versus care team on real messages
evidence.effect: RadOnc-GPT slightly outperformed the clinical care team in empathy and was comparable in completeness, correctness, and clarity; graders identified limitations including lack of context and hallucination.
evidence.quote: The RadOnc-GPT slightly outperformed the clinical care team in empathy, whereas achieving comparable scores with the clinical care team in completeness, correctness, and clarity.

evidence.title: AI-driven rehabilitation: evaluation of ChatGPT-4o for generating personalized physical rehabilitation plans in comorbid patients
evidence.outcome: Expert review of LLM-generated rehabilitation plans for suitability for use
evidence.effect: 72.00% of plans were 'Suitable for use with corrections'; none were 'Completely unsuitable'; conclusion: not yet implementable without expert review and modification.
evidence.quote: 72.00% of the generated plans were classified as "Suitable for use with corrections".

evidence.title: LLMonFHIR: A Physician-Validated, Large Language Model-Based Mobile Application for Querying Patient Electronic Health Data
evidence.outcome: Physician ratings of accuracy, understandability, relevance of LLM responses to patient record queries
evidence.effect: 210 responses rated by physicians; median scores of 5/5 for accuracy, understandability, and relevance; challenges noted summarizing conditions and retrieving lab results, with occasional omissions.
evidence.quote: A total of 210 LLMonFHIR responses were evaluated by physicians, receiving high median scores for accuracy (5/5), understandability (5/5), and relevance (5/5).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Language Barrier Application in a Simulated Health Care Setting: A Proof-of-Concept Study
evidence.outcome: Certified medical interpreter review of translation transcripts for errors
evidence.effect: Human-certified interpreter reviewed 10 transcripts (3597 words) and identified 23 errors (99.4% raw accuracy); 3 had potential clinical consequences but were minor ambiguities.
evidence.quote: There were 23 errors (raw accuracy rate of 99.4%).

evidence.title: Qualitative evaluation of automatic liver segmentation in computed tomography images for clinical use in radiation therapy
evidence.venue: Cancer radiotherapie : journal de la Societe francaise de radiotherapie oncologique
evidence.outcome: clinician review of AI liver segmentations
evidence.effect: Clinicians found that some high-Dice automatic segmentations still required correction before clinical use; no numeric rate was reported.
evidence.quote: In some cases, segmentations with high Dice scores still required clinician corrections before clinical use in the radiotherapy workflow.

evidence.title: Reproducible generative artificial intelligence evaluation for health care: a clinician-in-the-loop approach
evidence.outcome: Physician and pharmacist review of real query-response pairs for correctness, completeness, helpfulness, and harm
evidence.effect: Of 633 queries, 614 evaluable; SMEs evaluated 426 pairs. Correctness 95.5%, comprehension 98.6%, helpful 94.4%, two responses (0.47%) scored as potential clinical harm; pairwise consensus 60.6%.
evidence.quote: Results demonstrated high rates of response correctness (95.5%) and query comprehension (98.6%), with 94.4% of responses rated as helpful.

evidence.title: Large Language Model-Assisted Surgical Consent Forms in Non-English Language: Content Analysis and Readability Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Specialist clinician review of LLM-edited consent forms for risk, benefit, alternative content quality
evidence.effect: Specialist review detected declines in risk description (β=-0.371; P=.01) and overall impression (β=-0.500; P=.03) after LLM editing; evaluators found no explicit omissions but perceived text as overly simplified.
evidence.quote: The linear mixed-effects model confirmed significant reductions in risk descriptions (β₁=-0.371; P=.01) and overall impression (β₁=-0.500; P=.03), suggesting potential omissions in critical safety information.
evidence.sample_unit: surgical consent forms (liver resection) from 7 institutions, rated by 7 specialists

evidence.title: Clinical performance review for 3-D Deep Learning segmentation of stroke infarct from diffusion-weighted images
evidence.outcome: Clinician agreement with model segmentations (no significant error) and interrater agreement on retrospective clinical test set
evidence.effect: Clinicians agreed with DenseNet (DSC 0.831) more than U-Net (DSC 0.759): 83.8% vs 79.3%; interrater agreement 87.9% vs 72.7%.
evidence.quote: Our DWI segmentation tool achieved high performance with clinical review providing meaningful performance evaluation.

evidence.title: Improving radiology reporting accuracy: use of GPT-4 to reduce errors in reports
evidence.outcome: Radiologist review of GPT-4 suggested revisions for agreement, acceptance, and clinical harm
evidence.effect: Radiologists agreed with 27% of revisions and accepted 23%. Potential harm rare (8%), with 2 cases of potentially severe harm; 44% no and 46% low clinical impact.
evidence.quote: The radiologists agreed with 27% of the revisions and accepted 23%.

evidence.title: AI Opportunistic Coronary Calcium Screening at Veterans Affairs Hospitals
evidence.outcome: Cardiologist review of sampled high-CAC AI outputs for appropriateness of lipid-lowering therapy
evidence.effect: Four cardiologists verified that 527 of 531 (99.2%) reviewed AI-CAC >400 LDCT patients would benefit from lipid-lowering therapy.
evidence.quote: Four cardiologists qualitatively reviewed a random sample of the >400 AI-CAC LDCT patients and verified that 527 of the 531 (99.2%) would benefit from lipid-lowering therapy.
evidence.sample_unit: patients with paired gated and nongated CT scans (plus 8052 low-dose CT patients in a simulated screening cohort)

evidence.title: Enhancing predictive modeling for respiratory support with LLM-driven guideline adherence
evidence.outcome: Clinician chart review of LLM recommendations for guideline alignment, errors and harm risk
evidence.effect: 19/20 (95%) LLM recommendations aligned with guidelines; physicians agreed with 13/20 (65%); errors in 11/20 cases; 2/20 judged potentially severe harm.
evidence.quote: In a 20-case chart review, 19/20 (95%) LLM recommendations aligned with clinical guidelines and physicians agreed with 13/20 (65%) final recommendations.

evidence.title: Evaluating Locally Run Large Language Models (Gemma 2, Mistral Nemo, and Llama 3) for Outpatient Otorhinolaryngology Care: Retrospective Study
evidence.outcome: Expert ORL consultant ratings of LLM recommendations for patient safety risk on real cases
evidence.effect: Consultants judged LLM recommendations hazardous in 54% (Llama 3), 47% (Gemma 2), and 32% (Mistral Nemo) of ratings versus 1% for ORL doctors.
evidence.quote: ORL doctors' responses were considered hazardous for patients in only 1% of the ratings, whereas recommendations by Llama 3, Gemma 2, and Mistral Nemo were considered hazardous in 54%, 47%, and 32% of cases, respectively.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence applications for enhancing patient self-care education following sternotomy: Development and initial evaluation
evidence.venue: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
evidence.outcome: Research team review of AI responses to simulated patient questions as thumbs up/down/neither
evidence.effect: All 75 questions answered; 65 (86.7%) thumbs-up, 10 (13.3%) marked neither due to convoluted or incomplete information; none rated thumbs down.
evidence.quote: Of these, 65 responses (86.7%) received "thumbs-up" ratings, indicating that they were comprehensive, while 10 responses (13.3%) were marked as "neither" due to convoluted or incomplete information.

evidence.title: A Large Language Model Assistant for Summarizing Hepatology Referral Documents
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and hallucination rate of AI summaries reviewed against source hepatology referral records
evidence.effect: AI summaries had high accuracy (median 94.6% [IQR 86.5%-97.3%]) with a low hallucination rate.
evidence.quote: AI summaries had high accuracy (median [interquartile range]: 94.6% [86.5%-97.3%]) with a low hallucination rate.

evidence.title: Benchmark evaluation of deepseek AI models in antibacterial clinical decision-making for infectious diseases
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: Independent pharmacist review of AI antibacterial outputs against specialist regimens
evidence.effect: Five independent clinical pharmacists evaluated all outputs; DeepSeek-V3 had the highest overall ID specialists' endorsed rate, while R1 variants and ChatGPT o1 escalated to broader-spectrum tiers more than specialists.
evidence.quote: Then, Five independent clinical pharmacists evaluated all outputs.

evidence.title: Performance validation of large language models for drug-drug interaction consultations: Potential pharmacist assistant in outpatient pharmaceutical services
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Pharmacists Association : JAPhA
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM answers with pharmacist responses on real outpatient queries
evidence.effect: LLMs showed 84.85%-89.09% consistency with pharmacists' responses; discrepancies arose from incomplete pharmacist documentation, LLM drug misidentification, and differences in practical medication advice.
evidence.quote: The LLMs demonstrated high consistency with pharmacists' responses, with rates of 84.85%-89.09%.

evidence.title: Development of a generative AI agent for family support in implementing family-based treatment for children and adolescents with anorexia nervosa
evidence.outcome: Clinician review of AI responses for clinical appropriateness and safety
evidence.effect: Six clinicians rated 91.6% (437/477) of responses clinically appropriate; 8.4% inappropriate, mainly information insufficiency.
evidence.quote: The clinically appropriate response rate was 91.6% (437/477), including 92.3% for FBT-related questions, 88.0% for general knowledge, 93.7% for psychological distress, and 100.0% for other questions.

evidence.title: Initial Insights Into an Institutional Secure Large Language Model for Magnetic Resonance Imaging Examination Requests: Retrospective Study
evidence.outcome: Manual review of discordant sLLM outputs for hallucinations against real patient EMR inputs
evidence.effect: No clinically significant hallucinations were identified in a manual review of discordant cases.
evidence.quote: No clinically significant hallucinations were identified in a manual review of discordant cases.

evidence.title: Generative AI in Admission Notes and Diagnostic Completeness: A Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: CDI team adjudication of AI-identified secondary diagnoses in AI-drafted admission notes
evidence.effect: CDI team adjudicated 104 AI-identified secondary diagnoses, 97% (101/104) supported for documentation; principal diagnosis concordance 91% (20/22), AI misclassified principal diagnosis in two cases.
evidence.quote: The CDI team adjudicated 104 AI-identified secondary diagnoses, of which 97% (101/104) were supported for documentation.
evidence.sample_unit: matched pairs of AI-generated and provider-authored admission H&P notes

evidence.title: Large language models for optimizing clinical trial recruitment in ICUs: application to ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction
evidence.outcome: Expert adjudication of LLM-flagged potentially eligible ICU stays; positive predictive value
evidence.effect: Of 185 flagged patients, expert review confirmed 133 eligible (PPV 72%, 95% CI 65-78); estimated 86% reduction in clinician review time.
evidence.quote: Expert review confirmed 133 patients as eligible, resulting in a positive predictive value of 72% (95% CI 65-78).

evidence.title: Real-World Implementation of Large Language Models for Writing Clinical Discharge Summaries Within a Secure Data Environment: Development and Expert Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician-rated acceptability of GPT-4 discharge summaries (global confidence rating) on sampled real patient records
evidence.effect: 8/9 (89%) of GPT-4 summaries received a positive global confidence rating (yes or yes with minor changes); accuracy 7/9 (78%) for both sections; potential clinical harm results positive.

commentary.bottom_line: Clinician review of real inputs and outputs before full deployment repeatedly found errors, including tail-risk outputs that aggregate scores missed, but no supplied study compares deployments with and without such review. One pre-post study suggests tiered review may reduce potentially harmful advice, and the certainty of the evidence is very low.

perspectives.view: The record lists 67 studies as testing the practice. The 25 supplied are mostly level 3 or 4 single-arm reviews, and none compares deployments with and without pre-deployment review. One pre-post study reported advice with potential minor harm falling from 1.32% to 0.13% and 0.07% after tiered review. Design, indirectness, and differing criteria keep certainty very low.

Clinician review found problems that summary scores missed. In 50 neurology cases, aggregate ratings did not differ, yet 10% of LLM responses scored as concerning versus 0% of human responses. Other reviews found 5 misleading answers in 588 and one hallucination in 60 reports. Samples of 100 outputs may be too small to detect rare severe errors.

The choice of reviewer may change what review finds. Primary care physicians identified more omissions with greater harm likelihood than hospitalists did. Senior consultants graded more conservatively than an automated grader that otherwise agreed with ophthalmologists (Spearman rho 0.80). Three fetal radiologists reached an ICC of 0.93, which suggests predefined scoring criteria can yield consistent ratings.

Review at scale carries staffing cost. One program used 6,234 licensed clinicians to review more than 307,000 calls. In two studies, automated grading tracked clinician grading (rho 0.80, and P=.55 between clinician and LLM scores). This suggests a hybrid design could lower reviewer hours, though no study measured cost or time.

Two tests involved limited English proficiency settings. An offline review of 200 translated discharge instructions found variable translation quality. In a Nigerian vignette study, 17% of outputs were acceptable only with human review. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. A safety-net hazard study reported diabetic macular edema sensitivity of 26.5%.

A regulatory discussion paper suggests that reviewers consider whether a device performs consistently across clinically relevant subgroups. None of the supplied tests reported sampling reviewed outputs by subgroup. The evidence therefore does not show whether pre-deployment review meets that expectation.

In one hazard study, rheumatologists rated AI answer accuracy at 6.48 versus 9.08 for physician answers. Patients scored 0.49 on identifying AI answers versus 0.97 for physician answers. This suggests patients may not be able to screen outputs themselves, which leaves clinician review as a check made on their behalf.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied study compares harm reaching patients in deployments with and without pre-deployment clinician review. Such comparative studies are needed. They should also report how sample size was chosen to detect rare severe errors, how reviewer qualifications and criteria were set, and whether sampling covered clinically relevant subgroups. Studies should report reviewer time and cost as well.
commentary.underserved_note: Two tests of the practice involved limited English proficiency settings. One was an offline translation review and the other a vignette study. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, and hazard studies in rural, safety-net, and low-literacy groups do not test the review itself. Whether sampled review catches errors specific to these populations therefore remains unknown.
